issues.explanation: The bicycle trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of relief work in a war zone unless there is some specific event history linking bicycles to the trauma. The other triggers (unwanted thoughts, heavy breathing sounds) fit much better with war-zone trauma, making the bicycle item stand out as clinically implausible in this profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance implies a persistent current sense of threat, but the formulation explicitly isolates Threat as inactive, with no active links to or from the other nodes. In this profile, memory and appraisal are tightly linked, but a strong 'I have to be on guard all the time' appraisal reads more like an active threat belief than a memory-based negative appraisal, so it does not align well with the formulation structure.

vignette:
Margaret first arrived in the war zone as a relief coordinator, a job she had taken after years of municipal work because she believed she could make a tangible difference. She was fifty-three then, still single, accustomed to long hours and high pressure. What she had not anticipated was the night a mortar round struck the compound where she and her team were sheltering. She remembers the sound - not the explosion itself, but the heavy, ragged breathing of a colleague who lay beside her in the dark afterward, bleeding from shrapnel wounds. That breathing sound, wet and uneven, has never left her. Neither has the image of the man's face, lit briefly by a flare, his eyes wide and unseeing. She sometimes thinks that memory cannot be hers. It feels like a photograph she was shown once, belonging to someone else entirely, someone who was actually there. But then the images force their way into her mind without warning - during a council meeting, while she is reviewing a budget line, as she pours her morning coffee - and she knows they are hers, even as she wishes they were not.

The world, she has come to believe, is fundamentally dangerous. She does not say this aloud, but it governs her days. A car backfiring on the street outside city hall sends her heart racing. The heavy breathing of a man on the bus, asthmatic and labored, makes her want to flee. She has learned to avoid crowded places, though she cannot say why. She tells herself it is efficiency - she works better from her office, with the door closed. But what she really fears is the moment a sound will seize her, and she will be back in that compound, unable to breathe, unable to think. She has stopped attending evening events, citing scheduling conflicts. She has stopped walking to the deli where she used to grab lunch, because the ventilation fan behind it makes a thumping noise that reminds her of something she cannot name. Her colleagues have noticed. They say she seems distant, less engaged. She knows this, but she cannot explain it to them. If she thinks about the event, she will not be able to handle it. That is a certainty she holds like a stone.

She has also begun to feel that she will never feel normal emotions again. When a constituent thanks her for her work on a housing initiative, she feels nothing. When a friend calls to check in, she feels a flicker of irritation rather than warmth. She used to cry at sad news stories; now she watches them with a flat, hollow attention. This frightens her more than the intrusive images do. She wonders if the woman she was before - the one who laughed easily, who believed in the slow work of improving things - has been replaced by someone who merely performs the motions of a life.

What finally brought her to seek help was a council vote on emergency preparedness funding. She sat through the debate, but when a colleague mentioned the word "shelter," she felt the air leave the room. She excused herself, went to the restroom, and stood gripping the sink until her hands ached. She could not stop hearing that breathing. She could not make the image go away. She went home that evening and made an appointment. She is not sure what she hopes for. She is afraid that talking about it will make it worse, that the memory will become more real, not less. But she is also afraid of continuing as she is: a woman who once believed she could help others, now unable to help herself.
